response:
1. REFRAME

Your boyfriend is stating a preference he doesn't actually intend to act on, and using it as an escape hatch during conflict rather than as a genuine relationship demand. The real problem is that he has not developed the emotional regulation skills to stay present during arguments, and you are interpreting his retreat as a truthful declaration of what he wants rather than as a stress response. You need to decide whether you will accept a partner who abandons difficult conversations by threatening to downgrade the relationship, independent of whether he means it.

2. STAKES

**You:** You are investing emotional energy in someone who signals rejection whenever you encounter normal relationship friction. You stand to lose a year of your life to a pattern where vulnerability triggers his withdrawal, or to build resentment if you accommodate the pattern. You gain clarity about your own boundaries only if you name this dynamic and require change.

**Your boyfriend:** He currently has a relationship that meets his stated preferences (he says so explicitly outside arguments) but gets to escape discomfort by threatening to leave it. He stands to lose the relationship if you set a boundary he won't cross, or to lose the ability to use this tactic if you refuse to treat the threat as legitimate. He gains the chance to develop conflict skills he does not currently possess.

**The relationship itself:** It survives only if one of you changes—either you accept that threats are his argument style, or he stops making them. Right now it is in a loop that will exhaust you.

3. CONSEQUENCES

**If you accept the pattern as-is (treat his casual-relationship threats as his normal conflict style and move past them each time):**
You will experience repeated cycles of rejection-during-hardship, each time validating his strategy because it works—you capitulate or soothe him. Over 2-5 years, this teaches him the tactic works and trains you to suppress your own needs before conflict. The relationship may continue, but your emotional safety erodes. Moderate-to-high probability that you eventually leave not because he leaves, but because you burn out. Moderate probability he never develops the ability to sit with discomfort in a relationship.

**If you break up now:**
You lose a year and a relationship that otherwise meets your needs. You gain the ability to invest in someone whose conflict style doesn't involve conditional relationship status. You avoid 2-5 more years of the same cycle. Moderate-to-high probability you find a partner with better emotional regulation. Low probability you regret leaving if the pattern truly repeats as described.

**If you name the pattern as a condition and require him to change it (stay in arguments, develop skills, see a therapist, whatever form that takes):**
You set a clear boundary: "I need a partner who can fight with me without threatening the relationship. I'm willing to work on this with you, but I'm not willing to absorb your escape hatch." High probability he either commits to the work or you separate cleanly. Moderate probability he resists, claims he didn't mean it, or goes silent—in which case you get your answer anyway. If he commits and follows through, you have a relationship built on his capacity to tolerate discomfort rather than on your tolerance for his avoidance.

4. RECOMMENDATION

Tell him that you recognize the pattern—that he asks for casual relationships during arguments, then confirms he wants the current relationship when things are calm—and that you need him to stop using relationship status as an exit during conflict. Name it plainly: "When you threaten to go casual during fights, I experience that as rejection, whether or not you mean it. I'm not going to negotiate the relationship structure in the middle of an argument. If you want casual, we can discuss it calmly at a different time. If you don't want casual, then we don't use it as a pressure valve." Then stop engaging the threat when he makes it. If he brings it up during an argument, say "We can talk about this when we're both calm" and do not continue the fight around it.

The alternative—that he genuinely changes his mind only during conflict and truly means it each time—has some force; it would suggest genuine ambivalence about the relationship itself. But you have named explicitly that he contradicts himself, and you have also indicated through your own behavior (staying, not demanding change) that you will absorb the cost of his poor regulation. He has no incentive to develop better skills. Continuing to treat these statements as serious negotiating positions rewards the behavior.

The hard part: he may refuse to acknowledge the pattern, claim he "doesn't know" why he says it, or insist that this time he really does want casual. You will then have to decide whether to break up. That is the cost of setting the boundary. But it is lower than the cost of five more years of conditional relationship status.

Therefore: require him to stop using relationship threats as conflict management, enforce the boundary calmly the next time he tries, and be prepared to leave if he won't change. You cannot fix his emotional regulation by accepting it.
